seo.title: How to Make a Budget on Your First Salary
seo.description: Got your first pay? A simple, step-by-step way to budget on your first salary: know your take-home pay, cover the basics, save first and enjoy the rest.

h1: How to make a budget on your first salary
summary: Your first salary is a fresh start. Here is a simple, step-by-step way to build a budget on your first salary so the money lasts the whole month and some of it stays with you.
intro_html:
Your first salary is a big moment. After years of pocket money, part-time work or help from family, money now arrives in your account every month, and it is yours to plan. It is also the moment when habits form. The choices you make in the first few months often become the way you handle money for years.

The good news is that you do not need a finance degree to make a budget on your first salary. You need to know what comes in, what has to go out, and what you want to keep. This guide walks you through it in simple steps, with ideas that work whether you are paid in rupees, dollars, pounds, dirhams, riyals or euros.

sections.h2: Start with your real take-home pay
sections.body_html:
The number in your offer letter is usually not the number that reaches your bank account. Tax, pension or provident fund contributions, social security and sometimes health insurance are taken out first. What is left is your take-home pay, and that is the only number to budget with.

Look at your first payslip and find the net amount. If you have not been paid yet, wait for the first payment before making firm plans. Budgeting with the bigger "gross" figure is one of the most common reasons a first budget feels short by the middle of the month.

Check the pay date too

Note which day your salary arrives. Rent, bills and loan payments should ideally fall a few days after payday, not just before it. If they don't, ask whether a due date can be moved. Many landlords and service providers will agree.

sections.h2: List what has to be paid every month
sections.body_html:
Next, write down your fixed costs: the things you pay every month whether you like it or not. For most people starting work, these include:

  • Rent or a contribution to the family home
  • Electricity, gas, water and internet, or your share of them
  • Phone bill
  • Travel to work: fuel, bus or train passes, ride-hailing
  • Loan repayments, such as a student loan or a phone on instalments
  • Any money you send to parents or other family members

Sending money home is normal and important in many families, in South Asia, the Gulf and far beyond. Treat it as a fixed cost, not as whatever is left over. That way it is planned and respected, and it doesn't come as a surprise each month.

Then add the costs that change from month to month, like groceries, eating out, clothes and outings. If you are not sure what these will be, keep a simple note of everything you spend for the first month. Real numbers beat guesses.

The most useful habit you can build with your first salary is to save as soon as you are paid, not at the end of the month. Whatever is "left over" at the end of the month has a way of disappearing.

Choose an amount you can keep up, even if it is small. Some people start with a twentieth or a tenth of their take-home pay and raise it with each pay rise. Set up an automatic transfer to a separate savings account on payday so you never have to decide again.

What to save for first

  1. A small starter buffer. Enough to handle a surprise bill without borrowing.
  2. An emergency fund. Many planners suggest building towards three to six months of essential costs over time. Our guide on how much to keep in an emergency fund explains how to work out your number.
  3. Your own goals. A course, a trip, a wedding, a deposit on a flat or a motorbike. Give each goal a name and a target date.

You don't need a complicated system. Pick one simple method and stick with it for three months before deciding whether it works for you.

The 50/30/20 split

This popular starting point puts about half of take-home pay towards needs, about 30% towards wants and about 20% towards savings and paying off debt. It is a guide, not a rule. If your rent is high or you support family, your needs share may be bigger, and that is fine. Our guide to the 50/30/20 rule has worked examples in several currencies.

The envelope or pot method

Split your money into named pots, such as rent, food, transport, fun and savings. When a pot is empty, you stop spending in that area until next payday. Some people use cash in envelopes; others use separate accounts or the "spaces" feature many banking apps offer.

Try it with real numbers

Enter your take-home pay and your costs in the budget calculator. It shows where your money goes and how much is left for saving, and it stays private on your device.

You worked hard for this salary, and it is fine to enjoy some of it. A budget is not about saying no to everything. It is about deciding ahead of time what you are happy to spend, so you can spend it without guilt.

A few things catch many people out in their first year of work:

  • Lifestyle creep. New clothes, a better phone, more meals out. Each one feels small, but together they can use up the whole salary. Try waiting a week before any big purchase.
  • Easy credit. Credit cards, "buy now, pay later" offers and instalment plans arrive quickly once you have a payslip. If you use them, pay the full balance each month so interest doesn't build up.
  • Subscriptions. Streaming, gaming and app subscriptions add up. Review them every few months.
  • Keeping up with colleagues. Lunches, gifts and weekend plans can add up fast. It is fine to suggest cheaper options or to skip some.

If you notice you are buying on impulse, our guide on how to stop impulse spending has practical tricks that help.

sections.h2: Check in each month and adjust
sections.body_html:
Your first budget will not be perfect, and it doesn't need to be. Set aside fifteen minutes after each payday to look back at the last month:

  1. Did you spend more or less than planned in each area?
  2. Did any surprise costs come up? Add them to next month's plan.
  3. Did your savings transfer go through?
  4. Is there one small change you could make next month?

When you get a pay rise or a bonus, decide in advance how much of it goes to savings before you get used to spending it. Raising your savings at the same time as your pay is one of the easiest ways to make progress without feeling the pinch.

faq.q: How much of my first salary should I save?
faq.a: There is no single right amount. Many people start with a tenth or a fifth of their take-home pay, but saving something every month matters more than the exact figure. Start with an amount you can keep up and raise it over time.

faq.q: Should I give part of my first salary to my parents?
faq.a: That is a personal and family decision, and in many cultures it is expected and welcome. If you do, treat it as a fixed monthly cost in your budget so it is planned rather than taken from whatever is left over.

faq.q: Is it a good idea to get a credit card with my first job?
faq.a: A credit card can be useful if you pay the full balance every month, but carrying a balance can become expensive quickly. If you are unsure, wait until you have a few months of budgeting experience and a small savings buffer.

faq.q: What if my salary doesn't cover all my costs?
faq.a: Start by checking your fixed costs, such as rent, travel and phone plans, because they make the biggest difference over time. Then look at variable spending and subscriptions. If it is still too tight, it may be worth talking to family or your employer about options such as shared housing or travel allowances.

faq.q: Do I need a budgeting app?
faq.a: No. A notebook, a spreadsheet or a free calculator works just as well. The best tool is the one you will actually use every month.
